title: House price drop of 10pc in major cities, says NAB
full_text:
National Australia Bank has dramatically revised down its house price forecasts as the downturn gathers pace and spreads across the country, leaving analysts in its wake.
The bank expects Sydney and Melbourne's median dwelling values to fall 10 per cent, and mid-size capitals to fall between 2 and 4 per cent, from peak to trough. NAB forecasts house prices across all capitals overall to fall around 5 per cent. Only a month ago, its national forecast was for a 2 per cent drop, with Sydney down 6 per cent and Melbourne down 7 per cent over 2026.
Property prices in almost every mainland capital are in retreat, and the declines are accelerating - the national dwelling value fell by 0.7 per cent in July, the steepest single-month fall since December 2022, according to data provider Cotality.
NAB attributes its revised forecast to "slightly softer-than-expected outcomes for Sydney and Melbourne over recent months and a much sharper-than-expected slowing in Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide".
If the median price across capital cities combined fell by more than 8.2 per cent from peak to trough, it would become the biggest downturn in 40 years, as predicted by Morgan Stanley in May.
The upper end of the market in the two major capitals is shedding the most value as home owners at those price points have larger mortgages and are more exposed to reduced borrowing capacity when interest rates rise, analysts said.
Houses priced in the top third of Sydney's residential market - above $2.2 million - have already fallen 6.8 per cent in the past 12 months, a stark contrast to houses valued below $1.1 million that are still growing by 6 per cent annually, Cotality says.
The same trend is playing out in Melbourne, where houses at the top end - above $1.3 million but below the prestige level - have fallen in value by 6.7 per cent in 12 months, while houses below $765,000 have grown by 1.7 per cent.
Real Estate marketing platform Domain's worst-case scenario for this financial year is that Sydney's median home value will fall by $122,000 (7 per cent) and Melbourne's will fall by $84,000 (8 per cent). Chief economist Nicola Powell said the declines will be greater in the top quarter of the market. "We are likely to see the more premium end of the housing market see much deeper declines, and that could edge into over 10 per cent. I think that's quite realistic to consider that type of double-digit fall."
She said the pace of the falls in the last quarter for Sydney and Melbourne was unusual compared with previous downturns.
"This is the sharpest fall that we have seen in the first quarter of a downturn for Sydney ever on record," Powell said. "For Melbourne, prices have fallen for two back-to-back quarters. There's no other downturn that has been as severe in the second quarter of price falls as this one for Melbourne."
The suburb with the largest house price falls in Sydney in the past 12 months is the eastern beachside area of South Coogee with a 15.6 per cent decline, followed by Gordon (14.8 per cent) in the city's north and Wheeler Heights (14.3 per cent) in the Northern Beaches.
In Melbourne, nine out of the 10 suburbs with the biggest house price falls are in adjacent leafy eastern council areas of Boroondara and Whitehorse. Deepdene had the largest price drop at 17 per cent, followed by Hawthorn (14.7 per cent) and Balwyn (14.6 per cent).
The worst downturn since the 1980s was from 2017 to 2019 when the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority tightened its lending criteria for investors, causing prices to fall by 8.2 per cent across capital cities over nine months, according to Cotality.
Cotality research director Tim Lawless said values had fallen faster in the past two months than during the 2017 to 2019 downturn.
"I wouldn't be surprised if housing prices fall by around 10 per cent. That will be the largest decline over the past 40 years, at least," Lawless said. "This downturn is looking sharp, but it might not be short because we're not expecting the market to really turn around until interest rates come down.
"I think we're, really, waiting for interest rates to come down for the market to find a floor."
SQM research director Louis Christopher said an increase in listings coming into spring was likely to contribute to the price falls as supply is likely to outpace demand. Total listings are now 22.8 per cent higher than July 2025, marking the strongest annual increase in available housing stock in over a year. Sydney's properties for sale are 28 per cent higher than a year ago, and Melbourne's up by 42.8 per cent, according to SQM Research.
"We're seeing increases in both new listings and older listings. More properties are coming onto the market, but they're also taking longer to sell," Christopher said.
"Going forward, we can expect another rise in listings as we head into spring. That increase in supply is likely to put further downward pressure on housing prices for the remainder of 2026."
